Compare within-person and between-person correlations

Source: R/stats_correlate_levels.R
correlate_levels.Rd

Computes two distributions of correlations for every pair of variables, following Fisher, Medaglia and Jeronimus (2018):

Usage

correlate_levels(data, id, vars, time = NULL, lag_adjust = FALSE, min_n = 10L)

Arguments

data

Long-format data frame.

id

Person identifier column.

vars

Variables to correlate (at least two).

time

Optional column giving the order of occasions within persons.

lag_adjust

Remove first-order temporal dependence before computing within-person correlations.

min_n

Minimum number of complete pairs for a correlation to be computed, within a person or across persons at one occasion.

Value

A data frame of class idiographic_level_correlations, one row per correlation, with columns level ("within" or "between"), unit (the person for "within", the occasion number for "between"), x, y, n (complete pairs), and r. Summaries per pair are returned by summary() and by as.data.frame(x, what = "summary").

Details

  • within persons (intraindividual): one correlation per person, computed across that person's occasions;

  • between persons (interindividual): one correlation per occasion, computed across persons. Each person's series is ordered by time; the first observations of all persons form the first cross-sectional data set, the second observations form the second, and so on.

If group-level results generalise to individuals, the two distributions have similar means and similar spreads. A within-person spread that is several times larger than the between-person spread indicates that the group correlation describes few individuals well.

With lag_adjust = TRUE, within-person correlations are computed on residuals after regressing each variable on its own lag-1 value and the lag-1 value of the other variable, which removes first-order temporal dependence. The original authors repeated this step until the Durbin-Watson test was non-significant; a single first-order adjustment is used here. Between-person correlations are always computed from the observed values.

References

Fisher, A. J., Medaglia, J. D., & Jeronimus, B. F. (2018). Lack of group-to-individual generalizability is a threat to human subjects research. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(27), E6106-E6115. doi:10.1073/pnas.1711978115

Examples

lv <- correlate_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"),
                       time = "day")
summary(lv)
#>          x      y n_within mean_within median_within sd_within n_between
#> 1 efficacy effort       36   0.3637722     0.3587067 0.2498384       156
#>   mean_between median_between sd_between mean_difference sd_ratio
#> 1    0.5034717      0.5096236  0.1373181      -0.1396996 1.819413
